\section[la terminal]{la terminal — the terminal}

\label{lesson:ES-C652-terminal}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the berth, then the Spanish for to get off.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la terminal}
\textbf{la terminal} — \textquotedblleft{}the terminal\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Los vuelos internacionales salen de la terminal dos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{International flights leave from terminal two.}
\end{quote}

At an airport it is feminine: \emph{la terminal}; \emph{el terminal} is a device.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{terminal} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{terminālis} \textquotedblleft{}of a boundary\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{terminus} \textquotedblleft{}a boundary, an end\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la terminal}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la terminal}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la terminal}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for the berth, then the Spanish for to get off, then say \emph{la terminal} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la terminal mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The terminal\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[extraviarse]{extraviarse — to go missing, to get lost (of things)}

\label{lesson:ES-C652-extraviarse}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to get off, then the Spanish for the terminal.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: extraviarse}
\textbf{extraviarse} — \textquotedblleft{}to go missing, to get lost (of things)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi maleta se extravió en el viaje.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My suitcase went missing on the trip.}
\end{quote}

Formal; airports talk about \emph{equipaje extraviado}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{extraviarse} is built from \emph{extra} \textquotedblleft{}outside\textquotedblright{} and \emph{vía} \textquotedblleft{}way\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from Latin \emph{via}: to go off the road.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to get off, then the Spanish for the terminal, then say \emph{extraviarse} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[la aerolínea]{la aerolínea — the airline}

\label{lesson:ES-C652-aerolinea}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the terminal, then the Spanish for to go missing.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la aerolínea}
\textbf{la aerolínea} — \textquotedblleft{}the airline\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
La aerolínea nos paga el hotel por el retraso.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The airline is paying for our hotel because of the delay.}
\end{quote}

Also \emph{la compañía aérea}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{aerolínea} is built from \emph{aero-}, from Greek \emph{a\'{\={e}}r} \textquotedblleft{}air\textquotedblright{}, and \emph{línea} \textquotedblleft{}line\textquotedblright{}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{līnea} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la etiqueta]{la etiqueta — the label, the tag; etiquette}

\label{lesson:ES-C652-etiqueta}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to go missing, then the Spanish for the airline.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la etiqueta}
\textbf{la etiqueta} — \textquotedblleft{}the label, the tag; etiquette\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Pon una etiqueta con tu nombre en la maleta.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Put a label with your name on the suitcase.}
\end{quote}

\emph{De etiqueta} — formal dress.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{etiqueta} was borrowed from French \emph{étiquette} \textquotedblleft{}a label, a ticket\textquotedblright{}, from Old French \emph{estiquier} \textquotedblleft{}to attach, to stick\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[la mochila]{la mochila — the backpack, the rucksack}

\label{lesson:ES-C652-mochila}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for the airline, then the Spanish for the label.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la mochila}
\textbf{la mochila} — \textquotedblleft{}the backpack, the rucksack\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Solo llevo una mochila.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I am only taking a backpack.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Un mochilero} is a backpacker.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{mochila} comes from \emph{mochil} \textquotedblleft{}an errand boy\textquotedblright{}, a word borrowed from Basque \emph{motxil} (EtymDB); the bag was what such a boy carried.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
